clinician.trajectory_summary: A 43-year-old man with prior anal fistula surgery (10 years ago) presented with 4 days of acute right hypochondrial pain. Initial evaluation revealed elevated inflammatory markers (WBC 12,000/ml, CRP 20 mg/l), markedly elevated CA 19-9 (2016 U/ml), and normal liver function tests. Imaging (CT with IV contrast and Bili-MRI) showed suspicious irregular thickening of the gallbladder wall with porcelain-like appearance, raising initial concern for gallbladder malignancy. Surgical exploration 3 days after admission revealed a hard gallbladder with thickened wall and contiguous liver infiltration. Radical cholecystectomy (Glenn operation) was performed. Histopathology of the specimen demonstrated ulcerated mucosa surrounded by epithelioid cells mixed with rare giant Langerhans cells without caseous necrosis—findings consistent with tuberculosis of the gallbladder. Post-operative antitubercular therapy (IREP regimen: isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide for 6 months with intensive phase of 2 months and continuation phase of 4 months) was initiated. At 9-month follow-up, the patient was doing well.

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: Despite initial clinical suspicion based on markedly elevated CA 19-9 (2016 U/ml) and imaging findings of irregular gallbladder wall thickening, histopathology revealed granulomatous inflammation with epithelioid cells and Langerhans cells consistent with tuberculosis, not malignant cells. The clinical response to antitubercular therapy and good outcome at 9-month follow-up further support tuberculosis rather than malignancy.

While imaging showed gallbladder wall thickening, the histopathology findings of granulomatous inflammation with epithelioid cells and Langerhans cells are specific for tuberculosis, not acute inflammation or stone disease. The absence of Murphy's sign and normal liver function tests also argue against simple acute cholecystitis.

The histopathology findings combined with the clinical response to antitubercular therapy (IREP regimen) and good outcome at 9-month follow-up strongly support tuberculosis as the diagnosis rather than other granulomatous conditions.
